**AI coding research brief | November 6, 2026**

**1. [Built on Broken Assumptions (BOBA): Why Coding Agents Cannot Be Left Alone](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.02207) · November 1**

BOBA ran ten coding agents through 280 chains of 20 requests from 140 open-source projects. Even the strongest agent, Claude Opus 5.5, finished with all tests passing in 66.7% of chains, but only 55.8% passed every request when submitted without ever breaking a previously passing test. A coordinator checking only the final commit would miss that difference. Each request started a fresh conversation, and workers never saw hidden test verdicts, so the study measures unattended handoffs rather than the benefit of intervening.

**Quadratus experiment:** Replay dependent requests on the same checkout. Compare current handoffs with a verifier that reruns earlier acceptance tests after each patch and returns the first regression to its author. Give both workflows the same total budget. Score final success and uninterrupted correctness separately.

**2. [DistDebug-Bench: Can LLM Agents Diagnose Bugs in Distributed Systems?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03523) · November 2**

The benchmark covers 120 real bugs across 11 distributed systems. Its most useful result for delegation comes from a six-bug pilot: compared with giving the repair worker no diagnosis, giving it a diagnosis that accurately located the faulty code increased how often it edited a reference fault block by 38.9 percentage points and reduced mean API cost by 33.7%. Touching the right code is not proof of a correct fix. The diagnoses were selected by known accuracy; a live coordinator would have to judge their quality without the answer key.

**Quadratus experiment:** Give a debugging worker’s handoff three fields: suspected code block, causal explanation, and a probe that could rule it out. Compare against both a prose diagnosis and no diagnosis. Score the implementer on verified fixes and total cost, including diagnosis, rather than agreement on a file path.

**3. [From Watching to Steering: Enabling Human–Coding Agent Collaboration through Execution Traces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04466) · November 3**

VibeTrace lets a reviewer fork a run at the decision that went wrong and turn the correction into a reusable instruction. On 20 held-out SWE-bench Verified tasks over five runs, skills learned from traces plus feedback reached 68% pass rate, versus 65% both without skills and with trace-only skills. Compared with no skills, input tokens fell 23% and inference cost fell 15.5%. The test tasks came from related repository subsystems; the benchmark feedback was simulated from verifier outcomes. The modest pass-rate difference is weaker evidence than the paper’s headline might suggest.

**Quadratus experiment:** From a failed and a corrected run, save one conditional instruction explaining when the worker should change its decision. Compare it with sharing the successful transcript on unseen tasks, including tasks from another repository. Count the cost of creating the instruction as well as using it.

**Try first: catch the first regression before the next worker inherits it.** Freeze prior acceptance tests outside the workers’ writable checkout. Run them after every handoff in both evaluation arms, but reveal failures only in the intervention arm. Track how many later workers build on a broken state, whether the final patch passes independent tests, and the total cost per successful chain. This isolates whether timely feedback is worth its rework cost.
